title: “BE INTOXICATED ALWAYS IN HER LOVE”: BIBLICAL MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MEAN SEXUAL INDIFFERENCE
paragraphs: “BE INTOXICATED ALWAYS IN HER LOVE”: BIBLICAL MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MEAN SEXUAL INDIFFERENCE
Proverbs 5:19 contains a sentence so passionate that if many Christians encountered it without knowing where it came from, they might hesitate to believe it came from the Bible.
Not simply remain legally married to her.
Not live beside her for thirty years while your hearts slowly become strangers.
The Hebrew text is even harder to domesticate:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
“A loving doe, a graceful deer—let her breasts satisfy you at all times; in her love be captivated continually.”
The final words are especially striking:
“In her love… be captivated, exhilarated, even intoxicated… continually.”

The Hebrew verb שָׁגָה, shagah, is unusually vivid. Depending upon context, it can describe wandering, reeling, going astray, or being carried away. Here, within the poetry of marital delight, translations understandably reach for language such as “captivated,” “ravished,” or “intoxicated.” The Masoretic Hebrew actually places this language directly beside the physical delight of the wife’s breasts. This is not a later attempt to make Scripture sensual. The sensuality is already there.
And that should make us confront something.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians became more comfortable talking about adultery than talking about marital desire.
We learned how to say, “Do not commit adultery.”
We did not always learn how to say, “Delight in your wife.”
We warned people against pornography, lust, affairs, fornication, temptation, and sexual immorality—and rightly so.
But sometimes we forgot that God's answer to distorted sexuality is not the destruction of sexuality.
Proverbs 5 is not embarrassed by married desire.
The entire chapter warns a young man against the seductive path of adultery. Then, remarkably, wisdom does not merely tell him what he must run FROM.
It reminds him what he should run TOWARD.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Then comes the imagery of verse 19.
And immediately afterward comes the contrast:
Why, my son, should you become intoxicated with another woman?

The same verbal idea appears on both sides of the moral boundary. There is a kind of desire that destroys covenant, and there is desire that flourishes within covenant. Proverbs is not teaching the young man to become desireless.
It is teaching him where his desire belongs.
Biblical holiness is not sexual numbness.
Faithfulness does not mean becoming indifferent toward the body of the person you married.
Purity is not pretending attraction stopped mattering after the wedding photographs were taken.
The biblical vision is much richer.
And maybe somebody reading this desperately needs to hear that because you are married, faithful on paper, sleeping under the same roof…
But something has been disappearing quietly.

Then two exhausted people turn away from each other in the darkness, illuminated by separate phones, carrying separate disappointments, wondering when the person who once made their heart race became someone they barely touch.
There may have been no scandal.
And distance can become its own kind of grief.
This is where Proverbs 5:19 refuses to let us reduce marriage to mere endurance.
God does not merely say, in effect, “Don't sleep with somebody else.”
Wisdom calls a husband to delight in the woman who is already his wife.
Let covenant love become something warmer than shared paperwork.
But we must be equally careful here, because Scripture must never be weaponized.
Proverbs 5:19 is not permission for a husband to demand sexual access regardless of his wife's physical condition, emotional state, wounds, exhaustion, fear, illness, or dignity.
And 1 Corinthians 7 cannot honestly be used to establish one-sided male entitlement either.

He says the husband should give his wife what is due to her and the wife likewise to her husband. He then makes the astonishingly symmetrical statement that the wife does not exercise authority over her body independently of her husband—and immediately says the same thing about the husband's body in relation to his wife.
And when Paul discusses temporary abstinence, he describes it as occurring ἐκ συμφώνου—by agreement, by mutual consent.
Biblical intimacy is therefore not a license for coercion.
A husband cannot quote Scripture about his wife's body while ignoring Scripture's commands concerning his own sacrificial love.
Ephesians 5 does not tell a husband, “Make sure your needs are met.”
It points him toward Jesus Christ—the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
Christian marriage is not two consumers asking, “What am I getting?”
It is two covenant partners increasingly learning to ask, “How can I love you faithfully, tenderly, truthfully, sacrificially?”
Christianity does not teach that the soul is holy while the body is dirty. The scandal at the center of Christianity is that the eternal Son of God took on flesh.
Jesus physically rose from the grave.
Christian hope is ultimately resurrection—not escape from embodiment.
So why have some believers acted as though acknowledging physical desire between husband and wife somehow lowers marriage?
What Scripture does is place sexuality inside a moral architecture sturdy enough to carry its tremendous power.
And that means this article is not telling a hurting spouse, “Just have more sex.”
Some marriages carry wounds that cannot be healed with a date night and a Bible verse.
Maybe childbirth changed her body and she no longer feels desirable.
Maybe age changed his body and he carries embarrassment he has never admitted.
Maybe one spouse repeatedly experienced rejection until asking began to feel humiliating.
Maybe unresolved resentment followed both of you into the bedroom.
Maybe illness, medication, disability, hormonal changes, chronic pain, grief, depression, exhaustion, or years of unresolved conflict have affected sexual desire.
Those realities should not be mocked, minimized, or spiritually bullied.
Sometimes love looks like rebuilding trust one painfully honest conversation at a time.
Sometimes love looks like getting appropriate medical or professional help rather than accusing your spouse of spiritual failure.
And sometimes the holiest sentence spoken in a marriage is simply:
I miss reaching for your hand.
I miss feeling safe with you.
I miss talking without defending myself.
I miss the person I married.
I miss who we were before disappointment taught us to protect ourselves from each other.
And perhaps underneath all those sentences is another confession:
“I don't know how to find our way back.”
That is where the Gospel enters.
Not as a trick for improving your sex life.
Not as religious decoration around marriage advice.
The Gospel enters because marriage involves sinners.
You married someone capable of hurting you.
And they married someone capable of hurting them.
Sin does not remain outside the wedding ceremony simply because the vows mentioned God.
And sometimes the person lying beside you becomes the person who sees most clearly what everyone else never sees.
But scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Because Jesus Christ specializes in rewriting stories sin seemed determined to finish.
The cross tells the truth about us without abandoning us.
We were not rescued because we were innocent.
He does not heal us by pretending our sin wasn't serious. He carries its judgment, offers forgiveness to the repentant, and begins making people new.
That means a husband can repent.
The wounded can establish wise boundaries while healing.
The ashamed can discover that their worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
And forgiveness does not mean pretending consequences do not exist.
Reconciliation after serious betrayal may require confession, accountability, transparency, patience, changed behavior, wise pastoral care, and sometimes qualified professional counseling.
Grace tells the truth and then refuses to believe sin is more powerful than Christ.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Maybe your marriage does not need another performance.
Maybe tonight, instead of silently scrolling beside each other, somebody needs to put the phone down.
“I have rejected you in ways I didn't realize were hurting you.”
“I have compared you to people on a screen.”
“I haven't listened to what you need.”
Those sentences are terrifying because intimacy is not merely naked bodies.
It is being known without the costume.
It is allowing another human being to see the insecurity beneath the anger, the loneliness beneath the silence, the fear beneath the rejection.
And perhaps that is why so many people settle for counterfeit intimacy.
An affair initially seems to offer excitement without the accumulated weight of ordinary covenant life.
But counterfeit intimacy eventually collects its price.
That is why the chapter does not merely shout, “NO.”
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Protect what God entrusted to you.
And hear this carefully: “always” does not mean every marriage will permanently feel like the honeymoon.
Biblical love is deeper than emotional adrenaline.

There will be pregnancies, sleepless nights, financial pressure, screaming toddlers, demanding jobs, illness, aging parents, grief, body changes, misunderstandings, seasons of low desire, and days when romance requires deliberate cultivation.
It means covenant love refuses to surrender the marriage to indifference.
You keep making room for delight.
You keep remembering that your spouse is not furniture in the house you built together.
Someone who still needs to be seen.
And if you are unmarried, Proverbs 5 still has something urgent to say to you.
Do not train your desires on what cannot belong to you faithfully and then expect marriage magically to retrain them.
What you repeatedly feed becomes easier to hunger for.
Do not treat another person's body as content.
Do not confuse lust with love.
Bring your sexuality beneath the lordship of Jesus before marriage, not merely after it.
And if you have already failed…
The Gospel is not only for people who kept themselves spotless.
But sexual sin is not stronger than the blood of Jesus Christ.
You may have trust to rebuild.
You may have difficult confessions ahead.
But if you come to Christ, you are not coming to a Savior surprised by what you have done.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
No more blaming your spouse for choices you made.
No more using “everybody struggles” as camouflage for refusing to repent.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable prisoners.
And maybe this is where you need to stop reading for several seconds.
Because you know exactly what the Holy Spirit has been pressing on.
Maybe you haven't betrayed your spouse with another body.
You betrayed your covenant with neglect.
Stopped fighting for the tenderness you once promised to protect.
And now Proverbs reaches across thousands of years and whispers into a bedroom illuminated by two lonely screens:
By the covenant you already made.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn conviction into shame and then run from God.
You don't have to publish private details. You don't owe strangers your wounds.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack through which light enters.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
And we will not tell you that you cannot glorify God unless you give money to us.
Paul's instruction concerning Christian generosity is explicit:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ … μὴ … ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each should give as he has determined in his heart—not from compulsion.
ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ Θεός
That principle matters. Christian generosity is meant to arise from willing hearts, not spiritual pressure.
Your local-church commitments, your convictions concerning tithes and offerings, and voluntary support for a digital ministry should therefore not be deceptively collapsed into one category.
Send Scripture to somebody fighting temptation.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
There are many ways to participate in spreading truth.
Because in the end, Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A book cannot resurrect your heart.
A marriage article cannot manufacture reconciliation.
But Jesus can take two surrendered hearts, teach them repentance, truth, forgiveness, wisdom, patience, and sacrificial love, and begin rebuilding what sin tried to destroy.
look again at the person you promised not to abandon.
ask whether God is calling you to become different in this one.
ask whether tenderness stopped being cultivated.
ask whether you have become a safe, attentive, sacrificial lover.
Before using Scripture against your spouse…
And before believing your marriage is too damaged for grace…
Christianity began proclaiming hope from an occupied tomb.
Never underestimate what Jesus can resurrect.
Maybe trust has to be rebuilt brick by brick.
Maybe the first step tonight is not sex at all.
Maybe it is sitting beside each other without phones and finally saying:

And somewhere beyond the resentment, beyond the exhaustion, beyond the years that changed both your bodies, beyond the disappointments neither of you expected on your wedding day, perhaps you will begin to see again the person God once taught your heart to recognize.
And perhaps Proverbs 5:19 will no longer sound like an embarrassingly passionate ancient sentence.
Perhaps it will sound like an invitation.
Come back to delight without exploitation, desire without betrayal, intimacy without coercion, passion protected by covenant.
Because the deepest miracle is not that two imperfect people can remain attracted to one another forever.

The deepest miracle is that sinners can be forgiven, hardened hearts can become tender, hidden things can be brought into light, broken people can learn to love differently, and stories that appeared finished can be placed into the scarred hands of a resurrected Savior.
Your scandal may explain a chapter.
It does not have to write your ending.
Jesus still does some of His most beautiful rewriting in places everyone else thought were beyond repair.
